title: Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected
description: Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.The Argentinian
body: Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty. The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine". In a joint statement, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said that Buenos Aires must "respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future"."Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt," they wrote, urging Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory.The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law, arguing that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.Buenos Aires disagreed, writing in a statement after the decision that "Argentina did not ask the court to rule on sovereignty", but to apply the United Nations' sea laws to the UK over its "exploitation of our resources". It also said that five individuals would face sanctions for their involvement in the oil drilling venture, something Milei had been threatening. The statement did not specify who the sanctions would be against."The message is clear: those who participate in the illegal exploitation of our resources will face the consequences," the statement said.

schema.headline: Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected

title: Man arrested on suspicion of murder of girl in east London
description: A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murdering a 16-year-old girl who died in east London on Friday afternoon.Emergency services were c
body: A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murdering a 16-year-old girl who died in east London on Friday afternoon.Emergency services were called to a property in Grosvenor Gardens, East Ham, at about 15:40 BST following reports of concern for the welfare of a teenage girl, the Metropolitan Police said. She died at the scene.The man was arrested at Stansted Airport on Friday evening and remains in police custody. The Met said it believed it to be an isolated incident and the suspect was known to the victim.The girl's family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers. Det Ch Supt Jo Lloyd, who leads policing in north-east London, said: "Our thoughts are with this young girl's family and friends as they face an unimaginable loss."She said in a statement: "Neighbourhood officers will remain in the area over the coming days to provide reassurance and support. If you have concerns or information, please speak to them." Lloyd added officers were keen to hear from anyone who may have information, CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage from the area who has not yet spoken to police.

schema.headline: Man arrested on suspicion of murder of girl in east London

title: Channel 4 executive defends Huw Edwards documentary
description: Victims campaigners, politicians and members of the public have criticised the decision to allow Edwards to give an account of his actions.The Observe
body: Victims campaigners, politicians and members of the public have criticised the decision to allow Edwards to give an account of his actions.The Observer newspaper and Tortoise Media also interviewed Edwards for a podcast series to be released in the coming days.It will be the first time Edwards has been publicly questioned about the events which led to him leaving the BBC and later receiving a suspended jail sentence.Edwards, who was the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.He admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.Channel 4's Compton said Edwards "is not being allowed to tell his story unchallenged or on his own terms", adding he was not paid and had no control over the content of the film or questions he was asked.She said he had "never publicly faced detailed questioning about his criminal behaviour or the complete collapse of his career and reputation", adding: "There is a clear public interest in confronting him with those questions rather than allowing them to remain unanswered."Compton said: "Nothing about making this film diminishes the seriousness of that harm, nor does Edwards' participation entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation."Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, accused the media outlets who have interviewed Edwards of "not thinking about the victims". He said giving a platform to sexual offenders "gives them the ability to nail themselves to the cross".Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips criticised Channel 4 for giving Edwards a "platform"."Have they interviewed any of the thousands of other men who have been convicted of this crime to hear their side of the story or is it just interesting because he was famous?" she said to the Sun on Sunday."They should admit that the reason they picked Huw Edwards not any of the thousands of other men who have done this is because it sells, it's not about confronting the issue."Unless they had the express permission of his victims and they were part of the process it's just more platforming his voice while theirs remains silent."The interviews have also been criticised by three people who previously alleged Edwards behaved inappropriately towards them.One anonymous accuser, who said in 2023 that Edwards had sent them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel 4, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".Another who claimed Edwards sent them suggestive messages, while they were working at the BBC, said they were "disgusted", while a former junior BBC employee who previously said they had received inappropriate messages from him called it "strange and irresponsible".

schema.headline: Channel 4 executive defends Huw Edwards documentary

title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
description: Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.MSF sa
body: Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17. The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military." In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack."He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week. Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says

title: Rare quadruplets delivered by specialist 'quad squad' in Cardiff
description: Specialist 'quad squad' called in to deliver shocked couple's four babiesImage source, Cardiff and Vale Health BoardImage caption, All four babies hav
body: Specialist 'quad squad' called in to deliver shocked couple's four babiesImage source, Cardiff and Vale Health BoardImage caption, All four babies have names that start with N, in tribute to their parentsByChris WoodBBC WalesA specialist "quad squad" of 30 clinicians helped deliver a shocked couple's four babies.When doctors told Glenna Alphonse and John Poul Josh they were expecting quadruplets, the gobsmacked couple did not believe them and insisted the scan was wrong.But it was not, and in what was likened to "a military operation" they became one of only a handful of couples on average to have four babies in the UK each year.Following the one in 700,000 pregnancy, the two boys and two girls arrived earlier this month and were continuing to receive specialist neonatal care to help them feed and grow."At first, I argued with them, saying 'it's not quadruplets', said Glenna."But they took the scan a couple of times and called in experienced colleagues, and it was true."It gave us a big shock."Following what was described as a complex pregnancy, the babies were born at Cardiff's University Hospital of Wales (UHW) at 27 weeks.They weighed between 745g (1lb 10.3oz) and 1.18kg (2lb 9.6oz) and have since been moved to Singleton Hospital in Swansea, to be nearer the family home.As the common letter in Glenna and John is "N", all the new arrivals have a name starting with that.Image source, Cardiff and Vale Health BoardImage caption, Some staff members worked over shifts or returned from home to help with the birthsThe couple first discovered they were expecting quadruplets during a scan at the Princess of Wales Hospital in Bridgend.Because of the complexity of the pregnancy, Glenna was referred to Dr Bryan Beattie - the lead consultant for fetal medicine in Wales, based in Cardiff."At first we were scared," said John Poul."But we met Dr Beattie and he gave us very good support. He explained that the team would give us good care and told us not to worry about anything."He arranged counselling for us and that was very helpful."But following a routine scan at 22 weeks, the pregnancy took an unexpected turn."We were planning a baby shower and gender reveal party on the Sunday," said Glenna."But on the Thursday, at 22 weeks, we went for a regular scan."It was found that the cervix was close to opening. We had to cancel everything."Image source, Cardiff and Vale Health BoardImage caption, Most new parents are kept busy, but Glenna, John Poul and his mum Mary-Helen are set to have a bit more on their plates when the babies arrive homeGlenna was admitted to UHW and the specialist team worked to give her babies as much time as possible before they were born.So they did not arrive too early, a cervical stitch, known as a cerclage, was inserted.Glenna then spent five weeks in hospital with regular reviews."Mum was a brilliant part of the team. She was incredibly patient," said Dr Beattie."She was very, very uncomfortable and, from her point of view, it would have been nice to have delivered the babies long before."But she just put up with everything that we suggested in the best interest of the babies."A specialist team calling themselves the "quad squad" was formed and they put together a plan to deliver the babies.They prepared for two scenarios - an urgent delivery due to complications, or elective delivery by caesarean section, external. A theatre was identified, with space for each baby, while a specialist backup rota of medical and nursing staff was created in case of any issues.Image source, Cardiff and Vale Health BoardImage caption, The four babies are continuing to receive treatment in hospital When Glenna went into labour spontaneously at 27 weeks, the team's preparations were put into action."It was like a military operation," said Consultant Neonatologist Dr Rachel Hayward."A team of five neonatal staff was allocated to each baby, in addition to the theatre team plus NICU (intensive care) staff looking after the rest of the neonatal unit and attending other deliveries."Staff stayed beyond shifts, while some returned from home to offer support for an extra few hours."I had been struggling mentally, but after seeing my babies' faces the struggle was gone," admitted Glenna."It was totally, fully worth it."John Poul agreed, paying tribute to the team who "gave 200% for us".He added: "Everything was gone. There was only happiness."

schema.headline: Rare quadruplets delivered by specialist 'quad squad' in Cardiff

title: UK flu vaccine: Who should get it this winter and why?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesHealth officials are urging more people to take up the offer of a free flu vaccine as the number of hospital patients seriou
body: Image source, Getty ImagesHealth officials are urging more people to take up the offer of a free flu vaccine as the number of hospital patients seriously ill with the virus has risen sharply in the past week.The flu surge has come slightly early this year but that is not completely unusual. Flu activity is still at "moderate levels" and the peak may not arrive until December or early January, health officials warn.So what is the advice on getting a vaccine, who can get it for free and who should pay?How effective is the flu vaccine?"If you're offered it, it's a good idea to have it," says Prof Nick Hopkinson, professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London."The main reason is to avoid serious complications in vulnerable groups – so as many as possible should have it in those groups."People don't understand it's a potentially life-threatening infection and that the vaccine is safe."Flu is a viral infection which affects the nose, throat and lungs. Often it goes away on its own but it can make people seriously ill – complications can include pneumonia, heart attacks and other underlying illnesses getting worse.It can also kill.In England last winter, UKHSA estimated there were 3,798 deaths attributed to influenza.Scientists have to predict which strains of influenza will be circulating before the vaccine is manufactured each year in time for winter. The current one protects against three strains – two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain. Even if these strains drift slightly, experts say getting vaccinated is still a good idea to lower the risk of severe illness.Who is currently missing out?Millions of vulnerable people are eligible for the free jab to help protect them against flu, including children, pregnant women, care home residents, people with lung conditions and anyone aged 65 and over.But only around a third of under-65s and two-thirds of those aged 65 and over have been vaccinated so far this winter.That leaves around seven million people unprotected at present, health officials say.Parents are being urged to vaccinate young children in order to protect them and other people they come into contact with.Can I still get flu if I've been vaccinated?Yes. The vaccine does not rule out the possibility you will get flu, but it does reduce the chances you'll become very ill with it and end up in hospital.It takes two weeks for your body's immunity to build up after being vaccinated, which is another reason to have the jab sooner rather than later.Protection from the vaccine reduces the risk of serious flu complications by 50%, says Prof Hopkinson.If I'm young and healthy, do I need it?If you are not eligible for the free flu vaccine, you can still buy it from most pharmacies for between £15 and 25."It's a reasonable thing to consider," says Prof Hopkinson.But it is far more important for the millions of vulnerable people offered it free to be vaccinated. They are known to be at risk of health complications from the virus.Other groups are also at risk: "Smokers are five times more likely to get flu – so quit now," he suggests.Am I depriving someone else if I buy the jab?Simply put, no. There are different vaccines for those getting it free on the NHS and those paying for it privately.However, the vaccines do the same job and protect against the same strains of flu.Pharmacist Olivier Picard says he's seen a "massive spike in demand" for flu jabs in the last 24 hours.More people are booking an appointment for a free vaccine they have already been reminded about, and others are asking about paying for it themselves."When it gets cold, people tend to wake up to getting the free jab and want it before Christmas," he says.He says there is no issue with supplies of the vaccine at present and "plenty in the system".

schema.headline: UK flu vaccine: Who should get it this winter and why?

title: Carly Rae Jepsen: How GTA 6 gave her song Run Away With Me a second life
description: For years, Carly Rae Jepsen's fans have been telling anyone, external who'll listen, external that she wrote the perfect pop song... and they don't me
body: For years, Carly Rae Jepsen's fans have been telling anyone, external who'll listen, external that she wrote the perfect pop song... and they don't mean Call Me Maybe.No, it's Run Away With Me – three minutes of pure euphoria that captures the moment a crush snowballs into a full-blown love affair.Released in 2015, it stalled at number 58 in the charts, but it has long been a highlight of Jepsen’s live shows. Then, last week, it made a surprise appearance in Grand Theft Auto VI. It provides the soundtrack to a pivotal sequence where the game's protagonists get their first taste of the high life - zooming around on jet skis and shooting champagne bottles from the back of a yacht."Have I ever done that? I have not!" Jepsen laughs."My guilty admission is that I haven't even played the game yet, but I'm excited to try it. I'm gonna become a late-in-life gamer!"The placement has given the song a new lease of life. Its daily streams rose from 20,000 to 281,000 overnight. On Friday, it re-entered the UK charts at a new peak of 28."It's wild," says Jepsen from her home in Los Angeles. "I love a plot twist, and this was exactly that."In some ways, it’s a vindication for an under-appreciated classic."I've always been asked the question, 'When you were in the studio, did you know you had a hit song?'" says Jepsen. "And I always say, 'No. How can anyone know that?'"However, I will say, with Run Away With Me, out of all the sessions I've ever done in my life, we all felt that thrill that people think you get. We were on our feet, going, 'Oh, this has something special to it'."But it never got eyes like it's getting right now, and that makes me believe in that special feeling that we had, when we made it."The success comes at an interesting juncture in Jepsen’s career. Over the last decade, Run Away With Me and E•MO•TION, the album it featured on, have become cult classics, helping to establish Jepsen as a favourite among pop connoisseurs.This year, she rewarded her dedicated fans with a 32-track double album, Day & Night, that spans everything from mellow folk-pop to Abba pastiches and darker, dancefloor-centric experimentation. It was released as Jepsen, 41, welcomed her first child, Ilya, after falling in love with one of her co-writers, Cole Marsden Greif-Neill, during recording sessions.She told us more about the music, and her plans for touring with a newborn.In 2015, E•MO•TION was considered a commercial disappointment – but now it's considered a landmark pop album. How do you look back at it now?At the time, I remember feeling the pressure of having a song like Call Me Maybe take off. I was nervous about people expecting the same on repeat, knowing that I wasn't capable of delivering that. So E•MO•TION, to me, was a statement of like, 'Here's the type of pop music I love, and here's what I have to offer beyond [Call Me Maybe].'I'd set my expectations low. I'd taken a break and done Cinderella on Broadway. And when I finally put the album out, I was pretty sure everyone had forgotten what I did. So the fact anyone liked it was a victory.But did I imagine that it would catapult this new career path for me? I had no insight of that and, looking back at it now, I feel like it was like accidentally strategic for my [type of] success, which is finding people who want something true and authentic and artful, versus Call Me Maybe 2.0.And that freedom led you to a place where you can release a double album.Oh, absolutely! There are songs on this album that would normally be locked away in folders on my hard drive. On many songs, I felt like, 'Is this too weird?' But the mission statement with Day & Night was to stop asking that question.I notice you singing in new ways. You're almost whispering on After All, then That's Just Me is a classic torch song.Yes, it was actually really fun. My uncle and aunt were visiting from Canada, and they were like, 'Can we hear some demos?' And I played them some stuff, and they were like, 'I would not know this was you'.I felt like that was such a feat in its own right, to put out something fresh after so many years in the business.How did you decide what was a 'Day' song and what was a 'Night' one?The Day songs are more organic. Folky, psychedelic pop is where I would land with it. At night, we go a little bit more synth-based, like a dance party in my house.The first track you wrote was a 'Night' song: No Labels, I Love YouYes, with my partner, Cole, who's now my husband.Was that session the first time you met?It was, yeah, in the parking lot at Henson Studios. We were friends for a whole year before we started dating, but there was definitely some chemistry and excitement there. After that session, I was trying to save his contact details, and because the song we'd written was No Labels, I Love You, I wrote, 'Cole I Love You' in my phone. Turns out the joke's on me! I kept the contact in my phone that way forever.One of my favourite songs is Blue Skies, and the opening lyric is, 'I said I love you first'. Is that autobiographical?No, the funny thing is, we had a trip to Japan, and I had this big idea that I was going to tell him I loved him on top of the Tokyo Tower. I felt like doing something cinematic and ridiculous... but he beat me to it. He told me three days before when we were in Hakone, in the spa!So if the relationship was developing as the album was being written, has it become a document of that romance?I mean, there's a heck of a lot of songs that are dedicated to Cole, but there's other moments where I'm literally writing with him, and we're talking about something from my past, and those songs are threaded in there, too.Well, congratulations to you both. And congratulations on becoming parents, too! Your son's name is Ilya, right?Yes, Ilya. Weirdly, he is getting cuter every day, which is saying something because he started off cute. Every day, I'm seeing a new facial expression, like a new little nose scrunch or something. It's wild.Have you spoken to any other musicians for advice on touring with a toddler?I can get so much advice from my mom and my girlfriends about raising kids, but none of them have been on tour – so I spoke to Sarah McLachlan, who gave me loads of tips. But what's really in my corner is the amount of people, and women who have kids specifically, on this tour with me.So the way we've planned for time off, and even the buses we're picking are very suited for children. I'm not in it alone.How do you make a tour bus suitable for children?You need to have a place for the pack'n'play [travel cot]. You have to change how the bathroom is. But we're also looking at how we handle the long drives.I'm quite cockily talking about it with confidence before I've done a run. Catch me on the flip side and I might be like, 'Don't ever do it!'With 32 new songs, how will you plan the setlist? I know, right? We'll be like Bruce Springsteen, playing late into the night.I mean, we'll see how long my voice lasts...On top of everything else, you're also working on the musical version of 10 Things I Hate About You. How's that going?This is year six of working on that show, isn't that crazy?Musicals take a long time…They take a hot minute, but now we've had workshops in New York with actors and choreography and staging. What we're trying to do is honour how hilarious the story is. Because when I go to a show I want to cry, I want to laugh, and I want to leave 10 pounds lighter, feeling great about the world. If it can have all those things, it'll be a success in my eyes.

schema.headline: Carly Rae Jepsen: How GTA 6 gave her song Run Away With Me a second life

title: Swansea bride who went ahead with wedding after being jilted gets married
description: Jilted bride who went ahead with her wedding alone finally walks down the aisleImage source, Weddings by JACKsBACKImage caption, Kayley said being abl
body: Jilted bride who went ahead with her wedding alone finally walks down the aisleImage source, Weddings by JACKsBACKImage caption, Kayley said being able to hold Richard's hands and share vows "was everything I pictured and more"ByPaul PigottBBC WalesUpdated 25 November 2026A bride who became a social media sensation after being jilted at the altar has described the "pure magic" of finally walking down the aisle.Kayley Stead's fiance did not turn up for her big day in 2022, but she surprised everyone by letting the celebration continue with many agreeing to "just go with this madness".Four years on and she has found love again, reconnecting with an old university friend who did turn up for their ceremony on Friday 13th November. Stead walked down the aisle in a bespoke wedding dress to applause, later saying she felt everyone was relieved the wedding was actually happening this time.Marrying Richard Perrott was everything she had imagined, Stead told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast."As soon as I started walking down the aisle, everyone just started clapping, because I think everyone was relieved that this is actually happening," she said.Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Weddings by JACKsBACKImage caption, Richard and Kayley tied the knot after meeting at universitySlide 1 of 6, Kayley is wearing a white dress at her wedding. She has mid-length curly hair and a long vale. Richard is in a black suit. , Richard and Kayley tied the knot after meeting at universityShe described exchanging vows with Perrott as a moment when "everyone else just kind of disappears and it's just you two in the room"."It just felt magical," she added.Her new chapter in life was also marked by a change in style.Stead described her dress in 2022 as being "kind of like an armour, rather than a bridal dress".Image source, Neil Jones PhotographyImage caption, The guests at Kayley's previous wedding still made it a memorable occasionHer new dress, from designer April Brambury, made her feel "a million bucks"."I wanted a dress that celebrated my body, who I am as a woman, and I didn't want to shy away from that."She said being able to hold his hands and share vows "was everything I pictured and more".

schema.headline: Swansea bride who went ahead with wedding after being jilted gets married

title: Davis Cup: GB miss out on final as Spain's Carlos Alcaraz beats Arthur Fery after Cameron Norrie loses
description: Figure caption, Alcaraz sends Spain to the final with dominant win against FeryByEmily SalleyBBC Sport journalistGreat Britain were unable to give Leo
body: Figure caption, Alcaraz sends Spain to the final with dominant win against FeryByEmily SalleyBBC Sport journalistGreat Britain were unable to give Leon Smith the perfect send-off as Davis Cup captain as Carlos Alcaraz inspired Spain to a 2-0 victory in the semi-finals.Competing in their first Davis Cup semi-final since 2019, Britain fell short as Arthur Fery was unable to match the dazzling brilliance of Alcaraz, with the seven-time major winner surging to an emphatic 6-2 6-1 win.That was after rising star Rafael Jodar defeated Cameron Norrie 6-2 7-5 in the opening singles match to put Spain in the driving seat in Bologna.The defeat brings the curtain down on Smith's near 17-year tenure as captain, during which he led Britain to Davis Cup success in 2015.Spain captain David Ferrer, who is also stepping down after this year's tournament, will have the chance to guide his nation to their first Davis Cup title since 2019 when they face Italy in Sunday's final.Three-time defending champions Italy beat Spain in last year's final, although they are without talisman and world number two Jannik Sinner because of a wrist injury that will keep him out of the Australian Open."It is a second straight final, it is going to be my first Davis Cup final, I'll do whatever it takes to win," said Alcaraz. "It's something I have been chasing for a really long time, to be in a Davis Cup final."Figure caption, Norrie loses to Jodar as Spain take leadAlcaraz back to brilliant best against Fery as Norrie losesAfter Norrie's defeat by Jodar, Fery was faced with the mammoth task of beating world number three Alcaraz - a player he had never faced before.Alcaraz lifted his first ATP Finals title six days earlier, a triumph that completed his astonishing return to the sport following four months out with a wrist injury.And his return to top form was on full display as he dismantled Fery, ranked 32nd, in a dominant first set in which he dropped just two points behind his first serve.Alcaraz's movement and shot-making continued to dazzle the crowd in Italy and Fery could do little to stop the Spaniard's sprint to the finish line.Alcaraz started the season by becoming the youngest man to complete the career Grand Slam with his Australian Open triumph, and now has the chance to end the year with his first Davis Cup title, one of the few trophies he has yet to win.For Fery, who enjoyed his career-best season and a fairytale run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, it was another harsh reminder of the gulf in class between himself and the game's top players after he fell in straight sets to world number one Alexander Zverev in Thursday's quarter-final.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Great Britain had not reached the final of the Davis Cup since they won the tournament in 2015World number 10 Jodar has established himself as one of the brightest talents in men's tennis in 2026, having started the year outside the top 150.In the past 12 months he has made his Grand Slam debut, won a first ATP title and experienced a meteoric rise up the rankings, which saw him qualify for the end-of-season ATP Finals, reserved for the year's top eight performing men.He and Norrie sped through the opening games, holding serve until Jodar struck the first blow with a phenomenal cross-court return on the Briton's serve to take a 3-2 lead.The young Spaniard doubled his advantage two games later when Norrie ended a 29-shot rally with a plant into the net and Jodar calmly served out the opening set after 32 minutes.A double fault landed Norrie in bother early on, but he recovered well and broke back for 4-4 before Jodar regained control to restore his lead, wrap up the victory and maintain his 100% record in three meetings against the Briton.Italy sealed their place in the final with a 2-1 victory over the Czech Republic on Friday as Lorenzo Musetti starred in both his singles and doubles match to keep their title defence alive.

schema.headline: Davis Cup: GB miss out on final as Spain's Carlos Alcaraz beats Arthur Fery after Cameron Norrie loses

title: A clinic is offering to reassess ADHD and autism diagnoses - and hundreds of people are interested
description: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to beco
body: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officerByKate BowieGlobal Health Updated 11 minutes agoFreya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police."I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.Figure caption, Watch: Vilda says she ''didn't recognise herself'' as autistic and is happy the diagnosis has been removedThe clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Psychologist Sebastian Lundström runs the clinic, which operates one day a monthBarred from jobsLike Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present."This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach."We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families."Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed 'I was stuck'Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma."I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains."It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group."It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry."It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditionsFears about stigmaThe opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD."The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society."That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.'Magic spell'People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed"."It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to."The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis."Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: A clinic is offering to reassess ADHD and autism diagnoses - and hundreds of people are interested

title: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic
description: Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her."It's not like there's going to
body: Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her."It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.But the world of work has proved more challenging.For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities."I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.

schema.headline: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic

title: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip
description: The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-baring, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal docu
body: The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-baring, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal documentary.Discussing it at a private screening, she said it reflected the "fear, anxiety, uncertainty" shared by hundreds of thousands of people each year "who receive the words no one wants to hear" about having cancer.The documentary, Heal, being shown on BBC One on Sunday, couldn't be further away from a stiff upper lip. This is royal television without any palaces or carriages, it's an intense 30 minutes examining how "cancer strips everything away" and then a different kind of self-awareness emerges.It reveals more of Catherine's inner thoughts than any of her previous speeches and we hear more from her children than ever before."Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. You have to go through treatment and surgeries and everything. "But there's a much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. I think when you've had to confront your own vulnerabilities, you know, when you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite and in those moments, yes, a shift does happen," she says.Some viewers might be left in tears, others may think it's too schmaltzy - either way, they're going to be talking about it. It packs an emotional punch, even though it's more of a self-scripted, video diary than a conventional, journalistic documentary."This will be a documentary that most people can relate to and will admire her for doing. There is an emotional directness that's an unusual departure," says royal commentator Prof Pauline Maclaran, of Royal Holloway, University of London.Maclaran thinks it will connect well with the public, who will admire Catherine's "bravery".The documentary follows Catherine's Three Peaks Challenge, in which she climbed the biggest mountains in England, Wales and Scotland in a single day, and the cameras record her driving in between and her encounters with other climbers.This climb is a big mountainous metaphor for the difficulties, resilience and help of other people during the "scary, disorientating experience" of her treatment.At the summit of one peak she gets voice messages from her three children - George, Louis and Charlotte - who each in turn send their love in a way that shows the closeness of their family. They also all hug and kiss later, along with Prince William, with tears being brushed away.Those moments could be the emotional peaks that people will share, in a documentary made for the social media age.It's also probably the most we've heard directly from the royal children.Somewhere, the late Prince Philip will be scratching his head at how much the royals have dropped their tradition of privacy. Although we don't learn from the film the type of cancer or any details of Catherine's treatment."No previous generation of the Royal Family would have considered producing something like this," says Valentine Low, author and royal commentator."They would have been less willing to talk about illness and personal matters," he says.But this documentary is in keeping, says Low, with a generation "that's more likely to think in terms of whether there could be a positive message from the experience".Nonetheless, says Low, such a film-making approach, sharing their own chosen thoughts with the camera without an interviewer, still allows Catherine to "control the narrative".And there are questions that arise. She speaks of her cancer journey being a "pilgrimage" and the need to "spend time on our spiritual health" - and it makes you wonder whether there has been a deeply religious or spiritual experience as part of her recovery.There's a melancholy tone to the documentary, describing the impact of a "really dark time", and you wonder how this will sit alongside the expectations of her future royal life, when she will be queen.It could also raise wider questions about the treatment, waiting times and recovery support available to the great majority of NHS patients, who do not have royal titles, but whose needs are as intense.But we see Catherine in this documentary in hospital wards sharing experiences with other cancer patients and hearing about their hopes and fears. It's deliberately raw and unadorned in how it's presented.There are lighter moments too, joking with her brother James as they head up the mountains.Speaking at a screening, Catherine said the documentary was about "giving back" to people facing similar health worries and also to recognise the support of health services and charities working with patients and families.Proceeds from the documentary, like her Three Peaks Challenge fundraiser, will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, in support of the hospital where she received treatment.The open, empathetic tone of the documentary has been warmly welcomed by those working with cancer patients."Watching someone speak so openly about the fear, the hope and the long road to recovery can make a real difference to those going through it," says Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK."Her honesty will help many people feel less alone, and it will encourage important conversations about cancer in homes across the country."Ceinwen Giles, co-chief executive of Shine Cancer Support, said: "The film's honesty is what makes it so powerful. "By being open about her experience, the princess gives others a way to start their own conversations about how cancer affects every part of a person's life, particularly younger adults and those with young families."Catherine herself says that her experience has made her think about well-being in a much more holistic way, "not just about fixing what is wrong. It is about finding balance in how we live.""My hope is that this film will encourage compassion, showing the real value in standing alongside one another in the hardest of times," she says.Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

title: Afghanistan explosion kills 10 students and injures more than 100, official says
description: At least 10 students have been killed and 110 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, a spokesperson has told th
body: At least 10 students have been killed and 110 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, a spokesperson has told the BBC.The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, the spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.The province's culture and information director Sami ul Haq Bayan said the blast took place in a house near Shagai Middle School in Asadabad as explosives were being prepared for mining and blasting rock, reports AFP.The Associated Press also cites the official saying up to 15 wounded people remain in hospital, while the rest have been discharged after treatment.

schema.headline: Afghanistan explosion kills 10 students and injures more than 100, official says

title: GTA 6: The AI race to clone the world's biggest video game for PC
description: How gamers are using AI and leaked files to clone Grand Theft Auto 6Image source, RockstarImage caption, Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC ve
body:
How gamers are using AI and leaked files to clone Grand Theft Auto 6Image source, RockstarImage caption, Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6ByLaura CressTechnology reporterHot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem – and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.The developer has typically released Grand Theft Auto on PC long after its initial console launch – 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.This time it may not have that luxury – in part because of an apparent leak of files from an Xbox development build of the game, but also due to the rapid advance of AI coding platforms.These tools are being used to recreate or adapt existing games, sometimes within days, taking away the control developers have over their products.Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, Grand Theft Auto 6 saw record retail sales in its first full day of release, hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in historyBarely a week after the release of GTA 6, efforts are already under way to get an unofficial version playable on PC, although some projects have faced takedown notices from the game's publisher.For some gamers, it's an exciting prospect, despite the legal questions surrounding the process.For developers, it may be a warning: if a game as big as GTA 6 can be recreated, what does that mean for everyone else?Like 'looking at a painting and making your own replica'The recent wave of AI-assisted game recreation has been widely linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model, released in September, and to agentic tools such as Claude Code.Mark Brown, creator of the YouTube channel Game Maker's Toolkit whose own game Word Play was recently recreated using AI, said cloning largely took two forms: replication and reverse engineering.Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing one, possibly using screenshots or a description.This, he said, was similar to "looking at a painting and making your own replica" – something which is "a very close copy, but is ultimately a new painting".It's a particular issue among smaller studios, many of whom worry that AI makes it easier for others to copy their work.When indie developers Sodoj and Marco from the studio Robotonic noticed a version of their unreleased puzzle game 204Snake appear on the free games platform Yandex with the same name, they were "appalled"."The game was essentially the exact same idea, the exact same mechanics as we had, but with the art looking a bit off," Marco told the BBC.The duo were able to issue a copyright strike to Yandex and Google to get the copy taken down, but said it only felt like a "small victory".Image source, Archive Photos via GettyImage caption, Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing oneThe second approach – reverse engineering – involves working backwards from a finished game to understand how it was created.One way of doing this is decompilation, which attempts to turn the game's final version into something closer to its original source code. Brown compares the process to "taking a cake and somehow turning it back into the original recipe, with the exact quantities of flour, eggs, and milk used, so anyone can remake the same cake".Reverse-engineering projects have helped bring games such as Halo: Combat Evolved and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers. A related technique, recompilation, can help adapt a game that has been reverse-engineered to run on different hardware. This is one of the methods being explored in efforts to get GTA 6 onto PC.Coders wanting to attempt this with Rockstar's latest game face a difficult task because of its sheer size and complexity.Earlier in November, Cyberleek – a hacker or group of hackers – released what they claimed to be a near-complete Xbox development build of the game. They later leaked what they claimed to be the missing .exe file needed to launch the game.It gave those working on an unofficial PC version a crucial new starting point."Now people are using AI to try and decompile it, make a modified version that could run on PC, and compile a new version," said Brown.Image source, Rockstar North / Rockstar GamesImage caption, Reverse-engineering projects have made it possible to bring full games such as Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsersSince the leak, several groups have posted claims of their progress on platforms such as X, ranging from getting the game to boot up to making it run at a stable rate.One attempt seen by the BBC on X purported to have some of the game running nearly as smoothly as it does on console, albeit on a high-end PC.Accounts and sites have even sprung up to track the various attempts, excitedly sharing clips of the latest milestone passed and scoring their efforts.Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, have not confirmed the authenticity of the leaked build, and neither has responded to the BBC's request for a statement.However, Take-Two has issued take, externaldown notices, external of public projects aiming to port the Xbox version to PC on platforms such as GitHub."There are no remedies available to rectify this clear attempt to facilitate copyright infringement based upon Take-Two's copyrighted property," one notice stated. Tech Life: One hundred years of AILaura Cress talks to game designers who say their unreleased new game was copied using AI. And Shiona McCallum reports on a new AI police chatbot.Available for over a year
News of the leak has been celebrated by some gamers on Reddit, who resent having to wait for the PC release."Why should the PC players have to wait half a year if you can develop the game in weeks as shown so far!" wrote one gamer, external."Will be funny when the decomp runs way better than whatever Rockstar can make," said another.Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said part of the reason why games are often released on PCs months after consoles is that PC versions are "complex" with "different hardware configurations", as opposed to the more standardised set-up of consoles.He added there could also be a more commercial reason, as Rockstar can "have a second moment when the PC version is ready".In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, external, the chief executive of Take-Two Interactive, Strauss Zelnick, said while piracy was a "fact of life" in the entertainment business, it had until now been "less of an issue" for video games due to their "file sizes and complexity".However, Zelnick also reportedly told an investor Q&A that the company was "utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and... legal activities appropriately".When asked about the legality of reverse-engineering code, Dr Tommy Thompson, an AI consultant who presents the AI and Games YouTube channel, said the practice of decompilation exists in a "grey area" - until it "reaches a point where copyright and intellectual property [IP] are infringed upon". He added that decompiling code could be legal within limits, such as for educational purposes, but "as soon as you attempt to use it to redistribute or repackage existing software", then this is "largely illegal". "In most cases, decompiling or recompiling code is likely to involve unauthorised use of the game IP," said Aaron Trebble, a UK intellectual property lawyer for Lewis Silkin. Anyone who releases or sells a clone "will almost certainly be infringing [on copyright]", Trebble added, though he said the law on AI companies' own responsibility is still evolving. Anthropic has reportedly since told Claude Code to steer away from recreating specific existing games, external, saying this would breach its usage policy.Despite this, people are continuing to work on an unofficial PC game, hoping to make it playable before Rockstar releases the official version."Seeing as this has already affected industry giants with very deep pockets, the proverbial bear has been poked," said Brown. "We'll have to see how it reacts."

schema.headline: GTA 6: The AI race to clone the world's biggest video game for PC
